kcet|Chemistry|2009|43||0|0.s:
Isotonic solutions exert the same osmotic pressure, and since π = CRT at a given
temperature, that simply means the same **molar** concentration.
The urea solution is 6% w/v, which is 60 g per litre. Urea, NH₂CONH₂, has a molar mass of 60:
concentration = 60/60 = 1 mol L⁻¹
So the glucose solution must also be 1 M ✓
Check the w/v options for completeness. Glucose has a molar mass of 180, so 1 M glucose is
180 g L⁻¹, that is 18% w/v — neither 6% nor 25%.
This is the point of the question: equal **percentages** are not isotonic, because the two
solutes have very different molar masses. Only equal molarities are.
Neither solute dissociates, so i = 1 for both and no van't Hoff correction is needed.
∴ 1 M solution of glucose.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|45||0|0.s:
At 373 K and one atmosphere, liquid water and steam are in **equilibrium** — that is the
definition of the normal boiling point.
For any system at equilibrium,
ΔG = 0
Substituting into ΔG = ΔH − TΔS:
0 = ΔH − TΔS
ΔH = TΔS ✓
This is how the entropy of vaporisation is measured: ΔSvap = ΔHvap/T, which for water gives
40700/373 ≈ 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
The others are wrong: ΔH is certainly not zero (3) — 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ must be supplied to boil a
mole of water — and ΔE is not zero either (4), since the vapour occupies far more volume and
work is done pushing back the atmosphere, so ΔH = ΔE + pΔV with both terms non-zero.
∴ ΔH = TΔS.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|46||0|0:
Count the share of each atom that belongs to one unit cell.
**A at the corners** — a cube has 8 corners, and each corner atom is shared between 8
neighbouring cells, so each contributes ⅛:
A = 8 × ⅛ = 1
**B at the face centres** — a cube has 6 faces, and each face atom is shared between 2 cells,
so each contributes ½:
B = 6 × ½ = 3
Ratio A : B = 1 : 3
So the empirical formula is AB₃.
This is the face-centred cubic arrangement, and the same counting gives the familiar result
that an fcc lattice contains 4 atoms per unit cell when every one of those positions holds the
same atom (1 from the corners + 3 from the faces).
∴ AB₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|47||0|0.s:
The nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing, by both the inductive (−I) and resonance
(−R) effects, so it deactivates the whole ring. The question is why the *meta* position survives
best.
Draw the resonance structures of nitrobenzene. The nitro group pulls π density out of the
ring, and the positive charge that results appears specifically at the **ortho and para**
carbons — those are the positions conjugated with it.
So ortho and para are the most electron poor, and an incoming electrophile avoids them.
The meta position is not part of that conjugation, so although it too is deactivated by the
inductive pull, it keeps relatively more electron density than ortho and para.
Substitution therefore occurs at meta — not because meta is activated, but because it is the
**least deactivated**.
That distinction is exactly what separates option (3) from option (1).
∴ because it decreases electron density at the ortho and para positions.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|48||0|0:
Take the reagents in order.
CH₃COOH + LiAlH₄ — lithium aluminium hydride is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid
all the way to the primary alcohol:
X = CH₃CH₂OH, ethanol.
X + Cu at 300 °C — catalytic dehydrogenation of a **primary** alcohol gives an aldehyde:
Y = CH₃CHO, ethanal.
(A secondary alcohol would have given a ketone, and a tertiary one would have dehydrated.)
Y + dilute NaOH — ethanal has α-hydrogens, so dilute alkali brings about the **aldol
condensation**. One molecule's α-carbanion attacks the carbonyl of another:
2CH₃CHO ⇒ CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO
Z = 3-hydroxybutanal, the β-hydroxy aldehyde known as **aldol** — the compound that gives
the reaction its name, being both an *ald*ehyde and an alcoh*ol*.
∴ Z is aldol.
kcet|Chemistry|2009|49||0|0:
All four reagents convert R–OH to R–Cl, so the question is which is **best**, and that means
which gives the cleanest product.
(1) SOCl₂ with pyridine:
R–OH + SOCl₂ ⇒ R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑
Both by-products are **gases** and simply escape, so the alkyl chloride is left pure with no
separation needed. The pyridine mops up the HCl, driving the reaction to completion. This is
the Darzens procedure and is the preferred laboratory method ✓
(2) Dry HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂ is the Lucas reagent — fine for tertiary alcohols but slow
with primary ones, and it can cause rearrangement.
(3) PCl₃ gives H₃PO₃ as a liquid by-product, which has to be separated.
(4) PCl₅ gives POCl₃, again a liquid to be removed, and it is a harsher reagent.
The gaseous by-products are the whole advantage.
∴ SOCl₂ in the presence of pyridine.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|50||0|0.s:
Sulphonation uses fuming sulphuric acid (oleum), which contains dissolved sulphur trioxide.
The electrophile is **SO₃** itself.
It may carry no formal charge, but it is strongly electrophilic: the three highly electronegative
oxygens pull density away from the sulphur, leaving that atom substantially positive and
electron deficient, so the benzene π cloud attacks it readily.
SO₃ can also be generated in situ from concentrated H₂SO₄:
2H₂SO₄ ⇒ SO₃ + H₃O⁺ + HSO₄⁻
The ring attacks SO₃, and loss of a proton restores aromaticity to give benzenesulphonic acid.
Option (4), SO₃²⁻, is an anion and would be repelled by the electron-rich ring, and (1) H₃O⁺
is simply the acid of the medium.
Sulphonation is notable for being **reversible** — heating with dilute acid and steam removes
the –SO₃H group, which is why it is used as a temporary blocking group.
∴ SO₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|51||0|0.s:
Compare the bond orders.
C₂H₆, ethane — a pure single bond, order 1, length 154 pm
C₂H₄, ethene — a double bond, order 2, length 134 pm
C₆H₆, benzene — the six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, so each carbon–carbon
bond is an average of a single and a double bond. Bond order 1.5, length **139 pm**
So benzene's bond is shorter than ethane's but longer than ethene's — it lies between the two.
That single fact is strong evidence against the Kekulé picture of alternating single and double
bonds: if that were right, benzene would show two different bond lengths, 154 and 134 pm.
X-ray measurements show all six are identical at 139 pm.
Option (1), between ethane and ethyne, is too wide a range to be the best answer, and
ethyne's triple bond at 120 pm is shorter than anything in benzene.
∴ in between C₂H₆ and C₂H₄.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|52||0|0.s:
Dry distillation of a calcium carboxylate gives a carbonyl compound, and with a **mixture**
all three pairings occur.
The two salts are calcium formate, (HCOO)₂Ca, and calcium acetate, (CH₃COO)₂Ca.
formate + formate ⇒ HCHO, **methanal** ✓
formate + acetate ⇒ CH₃CHO, **ethanal** ✓
acetate + acetate ⇒ CH₃COCH₃, **propanone** ✓
Every product is built from an H (from formate) or a CH₃ (from acetate) on either side of the
carbonyl, so only those three are possible.
Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, would need an **ethyl** group next to the carbonyl, and no ethyl
fragment exists here — that would require calcium propanoate.
∴ propanal is not formed.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|53||0|0.s:
Two clues narrow it down.
The oxidation product reacts with **phenylhydrazine**, which condenses with any carbonyl, so
the product is an aldehyde or a ketone.
It gives **no silver mirror**, so it does not reduce Tollens' reagent. Aldehydes do; ketones do
not. The product must therefore be a **ketone**.
A ketone comes from oxidising a **secondary** alcohol.
Now check the options:
(2) CH₃CHO is already an aldehyde, and it *would* give a silver mirror.
(3) CH₃CH₂OH is primary, giving ethanal — again a positive Tollens' test.
(4) CH₃COCH₃ is already a ketone, not something being oxidised.
(1) (CH₃)₂CHOH, propan-2-ol, is secondary ✓
(CH₃)₂CHOH --[O]--> (CH₃)₂C=O, propanone — a ketone, Tollens' negative, phenylhydrazone
positive ✓
∴ X is (CH₃)₂CHOH.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|54||0|0:
Oil of wintergreen is **methyl salicylate**, the ester of salicylic acid with methanol.
The reaction is a Fischer esterification: the carboxylic acid is warmed with the alcohol and a
little concentrated sulphuric acid as catalyst and dehydrating agent.
C₆H₄(OH)COOH + CH₃OH --conc. H₂SO₄, Δ--> C₆H₄(OH)COOCH₃ + H₂O
So the missing reagent is **methanol** ✓
The Na₂CO₃ afterwards is a work-up step: it neutralises the leftover acid, and the ester —
being insoluble and pleasantly smelling of wintergreen — separates as an oily layer, which is
how the test is recognised.
Ethanol (1) would give ethyl salicylate, which is not oil of wintergreen. Phenol and NaOH are
not alcohols and cannot form this ester.
∴ methanol.
